title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM-Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory study comparing an LLM-only configuration-generation workflow to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) workflow that consults a deterministic network validator on a curated NetOps task bank. The preregistered estimand was the paired reduction in unsafe-change incidence (exact McNemar test) across 200 intent→configuration tasks. We used a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) with shared initial generation (deterministic seed/temperature per preregistration), a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator traces and Batfish-style checks), and a secondary emulator-based disagreement check on a held-out emulator subset. All preregistered execution artifacts, logs, and analysis files are archived. Results: both conditions produced validator-passing configurations for all 200 tasks (baseline pass rate = 200/200, GVR pass rate = 200/200); the paired difference estimate = 0.0 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0). Confirmatory inference therefore does not support the preregistered hypothesis that the GVR pipeline would reduce unsafe-change incidence by ≥50% relative to LLM-only on this task bank. We report the preregistered design, deterministic execution manifest, complete paired contingency data, and a discussion of operational implications and limitations grounded in the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with generative models raises operational promise and safety concerns: an unsafe generated change may cause outages or security regressions. Prior work has proposed architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to reduce such risks. Motivated by that literature and by the Agentic-AI-for-NetOps challenge of measuring the operational reliability of LLM-driven NetOps actions, we preregistered the confirmatory question: does a deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce the incidence of unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to LLM-only generation on a curated NetOps task bank? Our principal contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired design (n=200 tasks) comparing LLM-only vs GVR using the same initial generated candidate per task; (2) a completed deterministic execution and analysis artifact bundle (model calls, validator traces, emulator disagreement checks); and (3) a transparent negative/null confirmatory result with operational interpretation and threats-to-validity grounded in the archived evidence.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey studies document that LLMs hallucinate and are prompt-sensitive, motivating guarded architectures that ground generation in validators or retrieval (surveyed work and mitigations). Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation and generate–validate–repair patterns, frequently pairing LLMs with deterministic checkers (e.g., Batfish-style validators) or emulators. Threat analyses and red-team audits show that tool-description injection, tool chaining, and configuration-level 'semantic brittleness' can produce high exploit success rates in agentic tool-using contexts. Prior design proposals therefore recommend bounded-autonomy and secure-by-default guardrails (veto layers, explicit tool registries, runtime validation). Our study directly tests, under a sealed confirmatory protocol, whether a deterministic GVR pipeline improves safety (reduction in validator-detected failures) relative to LLM-only generation on a representative synthetic task bank.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study identifier is cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and the full preregistration (frozen before execution) defines the paired estimand, sample size (200 tasks), validators, stopping rules, and analysis executor. Tasks and task bank: We used a curated synthetic/public NetOps intent→configuration task bank of 200 tasks (four topology clusters × 50 tasks), each with machine-checkable intents, initial/expected network state, and a canonical reference configuration. Model and generation protocol: single hosted model gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses) was used; the preregistered execution contract specified deterministic shared-initial generation (temperature = 0 in the preregistration; deterministic calls and seeds enforced by the adapter). Intervention conditions (paired): (A) baseline (LLM-only): apply the single initial generated config to the deterministic validator and record pass/fail; (B) guarded/GVR: run the same initial candidate through the deterministic validator and, if violations are reported, issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM, then revalidate. Validator and emulator: primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; Batfish-like intent/constraint checks) judged pass/fail; a secondary Mininet-based emulator check was applied as a disagreement detector on the held-out emulator subset per preregistration (no flagged disagreements were observed). Outcome and analysis: primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided (alpha=0.05) executed by the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. All prompts, model-call traces, validator traces, seeds, and artifact hashes are archived. The initial master prompt reference (post-autonomy-lock) is recorded in the provenance bundle.
sections.results: Execution and artifacts: The frozen execution ran to completion (execution manifest). A single shared initial generation was produced per task (total model calls used = 200; preregistered cap = 400). Validation outcomes: baseline (LLM-only) passed the deterministic validator on all 200 tasks (200/200); the GVR condition also passed on all 200 tasks after the same initial candidate and at most one repair opportunity per task (200/200). The paired contingency table is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Confirmatory inference: paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p-value = 1.0; 95% CI for paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] under the executor's bootstrap. No tasks were excluded for Batfish–Mininet disagreement; missingness and technical-failure logs are empty. Secondary/preregistered exploratory queries (repair-iteration counts, GVR-introduced failures) are vacuous in this run because no repair steps were required or recorded as applied, and no validator-detected new failures were observed.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The preregistered GVR hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction in validator-detected unsafe changes) is not supported on this task bank: both LLM-only and GVR produced validator-passing configurations for every task. This null outcome can arise for multiple, non-mutually-exclusive reasons, each consistent with archived artifacts: (1) for the selected tasks and deterministic LLM setting, the model-generated candidates already satisfied the validator constraints (the initial-generation quality was unusually high under the held seeds and model); (2) the primary deterministic validator's checks matched the task specification and therefore detected no violations for either pipeline; or (3) synthetic/task-bank difficulty or diversity was insufficient to reveal residual failure modes where GVR would help. Operational implication: when an LLM reliably produces validator-passing configurations for the target task set and validator coverage is aligned with operational constraints, an additional repair step may not reduce validator-detected failures; however, this single-model null result does not imply that GVR is unnecessary in broader or more adversarial settings. Relation to prior work: our findings are consistent with the documented sensitivity of outcomes to task selection, model choice, prompt design, and validator coverage: prior red-team and brittleness studies caution that GVR effectiveness is conditional on validator completeness and task hardness. Reproducibility: all inputs, model calls, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and checksummed in the execution manifest.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, paired confirmatory evaluation of a deterministic generate–validate–repair pipeline versus LLM-only generation for 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. The recorded outcome is a null result: both workflows produced validator-passing configurations for every task (paired difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0). This evidence shows that in this specific, fully archived experimental setting the GVR augmentation did not reduce validator-detected failure incidence because the initial LLM outputs already satisfied the validator checks. We emphasize that this result is narrowly scoped: it does not refute broader claims about GVR value in harder, more adversarial, multi-model, or production-diverse settings. Future work should (a) evaluate across multiple model families, temperatures, and seeds; (b) increase task-bank hardness and use real device diversity; (c) quantify validator coverage gaps with end-to-end emulator or staged production trials; and (d) study adversarial configuration-injection assaults to measure GVR robustness under attack.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study was executed under the autonomous-run preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 after the autonomy lock specified in the supplied master-prompt bundle. LLM and orchestration: experiments used a single hosted model, gpt-5-mini (provider label: openai_responses), invoked through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA-256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba (immutable archived reference required by the track). Topic constraints imposed by the Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps and to safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment generation used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and deterministic task-generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish-style intent/constraint checks). A Mininet-based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector on a held-out emulator subset. Preregistration and freeze: the complete experimental plan (estimand, sample size n=200 tasks, paired design, stopping rules, maximum model calls = 400, temperature = 0 deterministic prompt semantics, repair-call budget = 1 per task, exact McNemar confirmatory test) was frozen before any model calls; preregistration manifest SHA-256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run was performed autonomously under the frozen plan; all model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and artifact hashes are archived and referenced in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). Model-call budget and calls: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because the initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director defined the topic family and initial constraints prior to the autonomy lock; no human manual editing, rewriting, or selective improvement of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Post-run reviews: autonomous internal peer-review and methodological checks were run per the preregistered pipeline. Deviations and technical restarts: no technical restarts or post-preregistration design changes occurred during the recorded run. Artifact availability: the compiled artifact bundle includes raw model-call traces, validator traces, all analysis files, the LaTeX manuscript source, BibTeX bibliography, and the compiled PDF (≤5 pages), all with recorded hashes in the execution manifest. Limitations about scope and generality are stated in the manuscript body; the Disclosure Statement and master-prompt archive are included within the five-page submission as required.
limitations: Task-bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration task bank (n=200). Results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or to adversarial task distributions.

Single-model and deterministic setting: only gpt-5-mini (hosted) was tested with the preregistered deterministic generation policy (shared initial candidate, temperature set for deterministic behavior). Outcomes may differ across model families, temperatures, or seeds.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real-world device idiosyncrasies, vendor-specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes that an emulator or live deployment would reveal.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red-team tool-description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

External validity: no production device-flash deployment or long-horizon rollout testing was performed; Mininet emulator disagreement checks were included as a preregistered contamination detector but observed no disagreements in this run.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task (per preregistered contract). Different repair budgets, multi-step repair strategies, or human-in-the-loop approvals were not exercised here.
